title: Without work
hookLine: unemployment is a wound, not a failure of worth
tomorrow: first paycheck: how much of it is meant to be given away?

lines: STILL STANDING, LATE IN THE DAY.
cards: So, what do you do? It comes up fast at parties, and for someone just laid off it lands like a shove. Jesus told a story about men with no answer to it.

In Matthew, a landowner goes to the marketplace again and again to hire workers for his vineyard. Late in the day he finds some still standing there and asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Why stand you here all the day idle?"
Their answer: "Because no man hath hired us."

teach.b: Notice what they don't say. They don't say they're lazy. They're standing in the place where work is found, waiting.
Nobody chose them. The landowner sends them into the vineyard, and at the end of the day pays them the same as everyone else.
Whatever else the parable means, it refuses to measure those men by the hours they managed to get.
The Catechism says it plainly: work is for the person, not the person for work. Saint John Paul the Second wrote that unemployment is an evil, and that those without work deserve real support.
A wound, not a failure of worth. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words.

Moses Maimonides, the medieval Jewish teacher, set out levels of tzedakah, giving to those in need, and put this at the top: helping someone before they fall, with a gift, a loan, a partnership, or finding them work, so they won't need to ask anyone.
Both texts guard the dignity of someone without work.

The honest difference between them: Maimonides's highest rung restores a person's independence, so they stand on their own; Matthew's landowner pays the latecomers a full day, a gift beyond what the hours earned.

how: Catholic parishes and Catholic Charities often run job networks and support for people out of work, and the Church prays for the unemployed in its intercessions; Saint Joseph is invoked as patron of workers.

o: a sabbath day when no one is allowed to work
being out of a job without losing your worth
choosing to retire early and rest at home

games.q: in the marketplace — tap the pairs.
p: paid the latecomers a full day

s: the idle workers in Matthew say they didn't want to work
they say: because no man hath hired us.
Maimonides puts helping someone find work at the top of his levels of giving
so they won't need to ask anyone.
the Catechism says a person exists for the sake of work
it says work is for the person, not the person for work.

games.q: a neighbor lost his job months ago and has stopped coming to block parties. what does today's lesson suggest?
o: invite him, and talk with him as who he is, not what he does.
wait until he finds work, so he won't feel awkward.
send him job listings and leave it at that.
games.why: the landowner went back to the marketplace and brought the unhired in. worth isn't a job, and dignity starts with being included.

practice: Say out loud the name of one person you know who's looking for work, or who's been told they aren't needed.
Then say one true thing about them that has nothing to do with a job: they're funny, they're kind, they make the best tamales. If you pray, hold them before God by name.

wordCard.voice: Without work. Out of a job and no less a person: a wound, not a verdict.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 20:6: idle, without work; the landowner's word for the men no one had hired.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: worth isn't a job, in the vineyard or anywhere else. Until tomorrow.
